clinicalPearls: An inherited arrhythmia syndrome causing exercise- or emotion-induced polymorphic or bidirectional ventricular tachycardia
Presents with syncope or cardiac arrest triggered by adrenergic stress, typically in children and young adults
The resting electrocardiogram and cardiac structure are characteristically normal
Most cases involve mutations in the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RYR2) or, less often, calsequestrin (CASQ2)
Exercise testing or ambulatory monitoring reproducing the arrhythmia is central to diagnosis
Beta-blockade is first-line, with flecainide, sympathetic denervation and an implantable defibrillator in selected cases
reference.pathophysiology: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is caused by abnormal handling of calcium within cardiomyocytes. Mutations affecting the ryanodine receptor or calsequestrin lead to inappropriate release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum during adrenergic stimulation. The resulting calcium overload triggers delayed afterdepolarisations and triggered activity, which under conditions of high sympathetic tone generate bidirectional and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. Because the substrate is functional rather than structural, the heart appears normal at rest.
additionalInvestigations: Exercise stress testing to provoke the arrhythmia
Genetic testing for RYR2 and CASQ2
Family screening and cascade genetic testing
redFlags: Exertional or emotional syncope or cardiac arrest
Documented bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
Family history of sudden cardiac death in the young
reference.prognosis: With beta-blockade and activity modification many patients do well, but the condition carries a real risk of sudden cardiac death, particularly if untreated or non-adherent, and some require additional therapies.
pitfalls: Relying on a normal resting electrocardiogram to exclude it
Overlooking family history of sudden death
Prescribing drugs that increase adrenergic tone
